classification.tone: Warm, sun-soaked, profane, wistful, and grounded

evaluation.positioning_hook: A Kansas teen uses her inheritance to drag her graduating friends to Hawaii and build the restaurant they dreamed up as kids.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional promise is immediate: friendship, escape, first adulthood, and a scrappy dream with a clear destination. The inheritance-fueled leap to Hawaii gives it an easy-to-sell engine, and the restaurant premise adds a built-in aspiration that can travel beyond a niche audience.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast in the graduation-to-airport-to-Hawaii run and stays legible throughout: five friends, one inheritance, one restaurant, one impossible leap. The story engine is clean and easy to explain in a sentence or two.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Lila’s decisive, slightly reckless leadership gives the film a strong center, while Joey, Elliot, Rhea, and Hunter each carry a distinct function in the group. Their chemistry is the real asset: the banter, the roles, and the emotional fractures all feel playable and actor-friendly.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar coming-of-age impulse and gives it a specific, cinematic shape through the Hawaiian restaurant dream and the group’s impulsive relocation. The boldness lives in the scale of the leap and the commitment to a youthful, profane, sunlit tone.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps moving with a clear sequence of decisions, setbacks, and small victories: graduation, inheritance, flight, location hunt, opening, inspection, and survival. The momentum comes from the group constantly having to solve the next practical problem while their emotional stakes keep rising.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of five recent graduates using an inheritance to open a beach restaurant in Hawaii feels fresh because it fuses youthful fantasy with real operational grind. It has that 'of course this exists' quality once you see the group dynamic and the setting.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world has strong texture in both Kansas and Oahu: the Midwest departure, the surf hostel, the beachside foot traffic, the permit process, the health inspection, and the local social ecosystem. The restaurant world is especially story-generating because the business details keep colliding with the characters’ immaturity.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is distinctly sun-drunk and profane, with earnest friendship, comic chaos, and real emotional ache all living in the same scene. The script can pivot from back-alley jokes to tearful confessions without losing its voice.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the party energy, the script is really about class pressure, family expectation, chosen family, and the fear of becoming the life you were handed. The final time-jump and the childhood flashback give the story a satisfying sense that this choice will echo beyond the film.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is built as a true ensemble: Lila/Elliot, Lila/Joey, Rhea/Hunter, Joey/Hunter, and the full-group dynamic all generate material. The restaurant setup makes every relationship functional and emotional at once, which is exactly what gives the film its engine.

casting_characteristics: Five young adult leads in the 18-22 range
Lila is Australian by background and voice
Supporting roles include parents, property manager, health inspector, and local surfer

notable_requirements: Oahu beach and beachfront business locations

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond basic cleanup and possible crowd/environment enhancement.
technical.sfx_needs: Small practical effects for fire, kitchen mishaps, smoke, and food prep chaos.

Taco Bell is referenced in dialogue.
White Lotus is referenced in dialogue.
The Bear is referenced in dialogue.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong festival appeal and a natural streaming afterlife; the engine is the group building and sustaining a restaurant while their friendships evolve.

cost.note: Contemporary, character-driven, and largely contained to beaches, homes, a hostel, and one restaurant with modest practical needs.

cast.note: The film depends on five young leads with strong chemistry, plus a few scene-stealing supporting adults.

location.note: Kansas, Oahu, airport, lake, hostel, and multiple restaurant/beach setups create a manageable but varied footprint.

content.note: Frequent profanity, underage drinking, smoking, and some emotional intensity keep it in a mature lane.

rights.note: Only a handful of brand and title references appear, with no major life-rights or IP dependency.

strengths.what_it_means: A manager can pitch this in one breath: a graduating Kansas friend group uses an inheritance to chase a childhood dream in Hawaii. That clarity is valuable because it gives producers an immediate emotional and commercial frame without needing explanation.
strengths.evidence: The graduation-night phone call reveals Lila’s inheritance, and the next sequence sends the group to Oahu to open La Kai.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble has real combinatorial energy.
strengths.what_it_means: Every pairing produces a different flavor of comedy, tension, or tenderness, which is exactly what makes the film feel alive. This is the kind of group dynamic that can attract actors because each role has a distinct rhythm and function.
strengths.evidence: Lila/Elliot’s quiet intimacy, Joey/Hunter’s kitchen friction, and Rhea/Hunter’s emotional push-pull all play differently across the film.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The restaurant is a story engine, not just a backdrop.
strengths.what_it_means: The business gives the film a built-in structure: permits, staffing, menu decisions, inspections, customer flow, and money pressure all create forward motion. That makes the movie feel producible and gives it a satisfying work-life texture.
strengths.evidence: The script tracks licensing, thrifted equipment, menu cuts, health inspection fines, and daily sales totals.

strengths.what_it_means: She has the decisive, slightly reckless energy that can carry a feature and anchor the audience’s emotional investment. The inheritance gives her agency, but her real engine is that she refuses to live a life chosen for her.
strengths.evidence: She organizes the group, makes the call to go to Hawaii, and repeatedly pushes the restaurant forward when others hesitate.

strengths.what_it_means: He’s loud, funny, volatile, and wounded in a way that gives the actor a lot to play beyond comic relief. The film keeps revealing that his bravado is armor, which makes him the kind of part that can generate real audience affection.
strengths.evidence: His kitchen swagger, his meltdown after the customer interaction, and his confession about his family all deepen the character.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone balances comedy with ache.
strengths.what_it_means: The script can be funny without becoming disposable, and emotional without losing momentum. That balance broadens the audience and gives the film a festival-friendly, crowd-pleasing identity.
strengths.evidence: The film moves from drunken banter and kitchen chaos to the beach confessions and the final childhood flashback.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Hawaiian setting is active and aspirational.
strengths.what_it_means: This is not just a postcard location; it’s a place that changes the characters’ behavior, business, and social life. The beach, surf culture, hostel, and local foot traffic all create a vivid, exportable world.
strengths.evidence: The group learns to sell to tourists and locals, lives in a surf hostel, and builds the restaurant around beach culture.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The film has a satisfying emotional thesis.
strengths.what_it_means: It’s about choosing a life before the world chooses one for you, which is a clean, universal hook for buyers and audiences. That gives the movie a strong aftertaste beyond the plot mechanics.
strengths.evidence: Lila’s final voicemail to her mother and the time-jump ending both underline the same idea: they chose the life they wanted.

whats_special.headline: This is a highly pitchable ensemble feature with a clean hook, a vivid setting, and a restaurant engine that keeps generating story. It has the kind of youthful, profane, emotionally sincere energy that can play as both crowd-pleaser and festival discovery, while giving actors a real group dynamic to sink into.

lead_characters.name: Lila Riviera
lead_characters.hook: Lila is the spark and the spine of the film: a young woman with enough confidence to make the impossible feel practical, and enough vulnerability to let the audience feel the cost of that confidence. She’s funny, impulsive, managerial, and emotionally open in a way that makes her feel like the natural center of a group. She’s also carrying grief, family pressure, and a deep refusal to live a life that feels pre-written.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a lead role with propulsion, charm, and emotional range — the kind of part that lets an actor be funny, commanding, messy, and moving in the same film. It sits in the lane of performances like Saoirse Ronan in Lady Bird or Kaitlyn Dever in Booksmart: smart, specific, and emotionally legible without ever feeling generic.

lead_characters.name: Joey Morano
lead_characters.hook: Joey is the loudest person in the room and, increasingly, the most emotionally exposed. He performs chaos as a lifestyle — smoking, swearing, cooking like a man possessed — but the script keeps revealing the loneliness underneath the swagger. He’s the kind of character who can dominate a scene with comedy and then turn around and break your heart.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a showcase part for an actor who wants to be magnetic, volatile, and unexpectedly tender. It has the same kind of appeal as Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea or Paul Mescal in Aftersun when the material lets the bravado crack and the hurt come through.

lead_characters.name: Elliot
lead_characters.hook: Elliot is the dry, observant counterweight to the group’s chaos — the numbers guy who can still be emotionally present, quietly romantic, and unexpectedly funny. He’s the one who translates the dream into a functioning business, but he’s also the one whose restraint makes every small emotional shift land harder. He feels like the person who sees everything before he says it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a great role for an actor who plays intelligence with understatement and wants a subtle romantic current running through the comedy. It has the easy, lived-in appeal of a Nick Robinson-type part in Love, Simon or a Paul Dano-style emotional observer role.

lead_characters.name: Rhea
lead_characters.hook: Rhea is the group’s emotional barometer and visual brain — organized, stylish, and quietly terrified of what happens when the dream becomes real. She’s the one who can sell the fantasy, design the brand, and then suddenly reveal how much she needs the group to hold together. Her tension lives in the gap between competence and fear.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong supporting-lead part for an actor who wants wit, warmth, and a real emotional turn. It has the kind of specificity that can play like a Haley Lu Richardson or Auliʻi Cravalho-style role: bright, grounded, and full of feeling without becoming sentimental.

lead_characters.name: Hunter
lead_characters.hook: Hunter is the quiet builder in the group — practical, anxious, and constantly trying to keep the physical world from falling apart. He’s the least performative of the five, which makes his internal conflict especially potent: he wants structure, but he’s also terrified of choosing the wrong future. His stillness gives the ensemble a needed counterweight.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that rewards restraint and slow-burn emotional work. It gives an actor the chance to play the grounded, observant center in a loud ensemble, in the same broad emotional territory as a Lucas Hedges or a Justice Smith type of performance.

director_appeal.hook: A director who loves sunlit ensemble storytelling with emotional bite and a strong sense of place.
director_appeal.detail: The material rewards someone who can stage group chemistry, keep comedy alive in practical business scenes, and let emotional turns land without overplaying them. It also gives a director a clear visual playground: Kansas flatness versus Hawaiian brightness, beach nightlife versus kitchen pressure, and a final time-jump that can feel earned and expansive.

buyer_appeal.lane: Festival-friendly coming-of-age dramedy with commercial streaming upside
buyer_appeal.detail: This fits the lane of character-driven features that can travel on premise, cast chemistry, and setting rather than spectacle. It’s producible, exportable, and actor-friendly, with a clean hook that can sell to buyers looking for youthful aspiration, friendship stakes, and a vivid destination world.

considerations.area: The opening is strongest when it moves quickly from memory to motion.
considerations.detail: The camcorder childhood image, Kansas departure, inheritance call, and graduation all establish the emotional thesis; keeping that early stretch lean and decisive will protect the film’s momentum and get the audience to Hawaii fast.

considerations.area: The restaurant mechanics are a major asset.
considerations.detail: The permit, inspection, staffing, and menu details give the film its engine; continuing to foreground those practical beats will keep the story feeling grounded and commercially legible.

considerations.area: Joey’s emotional turn carries real weight.
considerations.detail: His disappearance and confession are the film’s deepest emotional pivot, and the script already earns it; a future pass could continue to protect the balance between his comic volatility and the hurt underneath so the reveal lands with maximum force.

considerations.area: Hunter’s split between the dream and school is a strong pressure point.
considerations.detail: His quiet hesitation gives the ensemble a useful internal fracture, and the story benefits when that tension is allowed to simmer before it breaks. That choice keeps the group dynamic active and gives the final reconciliation more lift.

considerations.area: The final time-jump gives the film a satisfying afterimage.
considerations.detail: The one-year-later restaurant payoff is a strong commercial and emotional button; preserving that sense of earned growth will help the ending feel both aspirational and complete.

considerations.area: This plays in the indie-to-streaming feature lane.
considerations.detail: The footprint is contained, the cast is youthful, and the setting is highly marketable, which makes the project attractive for a modest-budget feature strategy with festival launch potential.

considerations.area: The brand references are light but present.
considerations.detail: A few recognizable names appear in dialogue and background detail, so a production pass should keep an eye on clearance while preserving the script’s contemporary texture.
